Theme

Latin word

gravis

gravis, grave

adjective, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

dignified, serious, weighty (of a person or manner); serious, dignified; heavy; weighty, important, serious; major, serious, weighty; serious, dignified, weighty (of a person: the opposite of levis); serious, grave, heavy (of an illness, a wound, a danger)

In this lexicon

  • dignified

    the recommended word · classical · Traupman 304

  • dignity

    also used · classical · Traupman 151, 153

  • heavy

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. N.D. 3.83: aestāte grave esse aureum amiculum, hieme frīgidum (Lewis & Short); Hor. S. 1.9.21: cum gravius dorsō subiit onus

  • important

    also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.103: cum gravibus sēriīsque rēbus satis fēcerimus; M-O s.v. important

  • major

    the recommended word · classical · Liv. 34.17.12: gravem atque opulentam cīvitātem, “a major and wealthy city” (Lewis & Short); Cic. Rep. 1.3: gravissima cīvitās (Lewis & Short); Traupman 323

  • serious

    also used · classical · Cic. Lael. 95: inter … levem cīvem, et inter cōnstantem et vērum et gravem; Traupman 157, 376

  • serious

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. Cat. 1.31: hominēs aegrī morbō gravī; Liv. 21.48.4: gravis vulnere, badly wounded (Lewis & Short); Traupman 64, 331: gravis valētūdō, a serious illness

  • sevērus et gravis: formal

    classical

Examples

  • dēmittō auriculās, ut inīquae mentis asellus, cum gravius dorsō subiit onus

    I let my ears droop, like a sulky donkey when a heavier load has been put on his backHor. S. 1.9.20–21

    In the entry for heavy

  • vēnālēs umerō fascēs portābat in urbem: inde domum cervīce levis, gravis aere redībat

    he carried bundles on his shoulder to sell in town, and came home light in the neck and heavy with moneyMor. 81–82

    In the entry for heavy

  • ingeniī signum in parvīs praecipuum memoria est

    in little children the major sign of talent is memoryQuint. 1.3.1

    In the entry for major

  • major ignōtārum rērum est terror

    the unknown frightens us moreLiv. 28.44.3

    In the entry for major

  • ut saepe hominēs aegrī morbō gravī, cum aestū febrīque jactantur, sī aquam gelidam biberunt, prīmō relevārī videntur, deinde multō gravius vehementiusque adflīctantur

    as people with a serious illness, tossing in the heat of a fever, often seem relieved at first if they drink cold water, and are then struck down far more heavily and violentlyCic. Cat. 1.31

    In the entry for serious

  • sī cōnstituerīs cuipiam tē advocātum in rem praesentem esse ventūrum atque interim graviter aegrōtāre fīlius coeperit, nōn sit contrā officium nōn facere quod dīxerīs

    if you have promised someone to come and support him on the spot, and meanwhile your son falls seriously ill, it is no breach of duty not to do what you saidCic. Off. 1.32

    In the entry for serious
